rv.q: This is a suspenseful, beautifully staged adultery-and-murder thriller that, with the emotionally translucent Keira Knightley making her Broadway debut in the title role, left me feeling as if I had been somewhere faraway for just under three hours.
Cabnet's production does atmospheric justice to Thérèse's desperation.
The physical production is exquisite, and by the end of the act the performers have found the raw passion to leave the audience gasping.

Although the actors are magnetic and the Grand Guignol-accented story deliciously juicy, the play veers into overblown histrionics as Therese’s hallucinations assume the full-on haunted-house effect of fingernails screeching on a blackboard.
But no skill anyone might apply can reverse the trajectory of a story that dries up just when it gets juicy.

But it’s the vaunted arc of Zola’s 1867 novel to culminate in a body count that begins to rival that of Hamlet but without much – in this re-telling by British playwright Helen Edmundson – in the way of nuanced introspection.
This production never feels vital enough to care about anyone, no matter how much panting Knightley does.
But it doesn't feel like an entirely secure performance because, well, it is not fully connected to anything else on view.
Like these characters’ lives, their erotic encounters are nasty, brutish and short.

Any way you gnaw it, though, “Thérèse Raquin” is a dreary hambone that once was shocking but is now quaint, and Helen Edmundson, whose sole previous Broadway credit was the inept 2007 stage version of “Coram Boy,” has done no better by Zola.

The sky and the water and the very walls feel like characters themselves, and contribute almost as much as Keira Knightley’s compelling performance to this magnetic story of a woman trapped in a loveless arrangement, who is set free, only to be trapped once more by guilt.
The show is beautifully awful, splendidly agonizing.
I never got a sense of her Thérèse as deeply miserable.
When she’s wholly dramatic, as in “Anna Karenina” or this “Therese Raquin,” she’s monotonous.
It is another to lock us all in the basement with the characters until we get the feeling that there is no way out.
Without high heat and funky musk, this wannabe erotic thriller starring Keira Knightley is bloodless and all wet.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Play

cn.t: Mixed reviews greet this uneven revival, with critics praising the striking design but finding the production lacks sexual heat and tension. Knightley's performance divides opinion in her Broadway debut.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
